title: Regional contingency matrix and model slimming notes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working note to capture an operationally pragmatic approach to multi-region contingency handling and an additional idea weve been informally calling "model slimming": lightweight model fallbacks + tiered capacity exchange. The aim is to:
- define a compact contingency matrix (region x capacity state x model family) that the control plane can consume,
- outline heuristics for selecting slimmed model variants when primary capacity is constrained,
- propose observable signals, and
- surface open questions and short-term action items.

High-level principle summary (TL;DR):
- Prefer local region first, then lightweight regional spillover before global failover.
- Use model-slimming (quantized / distilled variants) as a middle tier rather than jumping directly to lowest-quality model families.
- Enforce SLO envelopes at the route level (latency/quality/cost) and treat fallback decisions as policy => control-plane evaluation.
- Keep fallbacks predictable: static matrix + scoring heuristics (not purely ad-hoc routing).

Vocabulary / shorthand used in this doc:
- primary: the normal model variant pinned for a customer/route (e.g., redwood-7b-fp16).
- slim: a reduced-cost/smaller variant intended to preserve fidelity (e.g., redwood-7b-4bit, distilled-3b).
- spill: moving requests to another region/pool.
- hard_fail: last-resort behaviour (reject or queue).

Contingency matrix (concept):
Rows: local-capacity-state = {normal, degraded-20, degraded-50, saturated} (percent of normal capacity available)
Cols: region-state = {local-up, peer-up, peer-constrained, global-constrained}
Cell contents: ordered list of candidate actions with priority and cost/quality estimates, example cell entries:
- (normal, local-up): [primary-local]
- (degraded-20, local-up): [primary-local-with-prefetch, slim-local, route-to-peer-lowlatency]
- (saturated, peer-constrained): [slim-peer, rate-limited-queue, hard_fail-to-caller]
Each action annotated with: expected-p95-latency, relative-per-token-cost, quality-delta (0..1 scale), and kv-cache-warmup-penalty estimate.

Model slimming: what and why
Rationale: binary fallbacks (full model vs smallest model) cause abrupt quality cliffs & customer surprises. Model slimming is an intermediate set of variants that trade a small quality delta for a large cost/latency improvement. Examples:
- precision-reduction path: fp16 -> bfloat16 -> 8-bit -> 4-bit; each step quantified for expected token throughput gain and mean token-likelihood delta.
- architecture-distill path: redwood-7b -> redwood-5.5b-distilled -> redwood-3b-distilled; steeper quality drop but lower compute.
- sequence-trimming: enforce shorter max-length preemptive truncation for non-essential requests in stressed state.
Operationally we currently target 2-3 slim steps per primary family. Each slim step should be benchmarked per-route by our Optimize product (or local perf harness) and have a labelled quality-cost profile.

Routing heuristics (control-plane duties)
Inputs available to the control plane per route/request:
- route SLOs (latency p95, min-acceptable-quality), billing tier, customer preferences (no spillover, no cross-border), pinned versions, token budget.
- real-time capacity signals: local GPU pool utilization, queued items, backend error rate, avg-kv-cache-hit-rate.
- historical model-profile for prompt-length distribution and cache hit distribution.

Decision algorithm (sketch):
1) Check route-level hard constraints: if spillover forbidden or data-residency flagged => only local actions (slim/local-queue/hard-fail).
2) Evaluate local pool headroom vs request's latency allowance. If headroom >= threshold => primary-local.
3) Else try slim-local option(s) in order of smallest quality impact. Use precomputed quality delta; if quality meets route min then choose.
4) If slim-local unacceptable or slow (e.g., warming KV cache would exceed latency budget), attempt spill to peer region that has allowed spillover and minimal added network RTT. Prefer peers with warmed KV caches for the same model-family.
5) If spill not available, consider controlled-rate rejection or degraded-response (shorter completions, ephemeral summary fallback).
6) Log decision + reason code; emit metric for decision category for downstream SLO and billing reconciliation.

Priority envelopes and rate-limiting
- Maintain a route-priority envelope per customer which is a small list of token budget + failover preference. In shortage, lower priority routes are nudged to slim variants earlier.
- Implement local token-bucket throttles per model-family to prevent thundering herds when spillover opens.

Cache and KV considerations
- KV-cache warmup is the single largest hidden latency when switching variants/regions. The control plane should add a KV-warmup cost to any candidate action.
- Warm-standbys: keep a tiny warm pool of slim-local replicas (one or two instances) for high-QPS routes so switch is near-instant. Cost trade: small always-on pool vs slower cold start.

Observability and signals to capture
- Decision metrics: {route_id, reason_code, chosen_action, expected_quality_delta, latency_budget_ms}.
- Latency breakdown: edge+network, model-init, kv-warm, token-gen.
- Quality regression signals: automatic sampled evaluations of outputs when slim variants are used for a non-trivial % of requests. Periodic A/B evals to detect drift.
- Alerting: if % of requests using slim variants > X% for > Y minutes for tiered customers => paging on-call + product notify.

Customer safety & transparency
- For enterprise customers, allow a per-tenant policy override: "never spill", "allow-slim-local-only", "allow-cross-border". These should be stored as route-level metadata and honored by control-plane.
- Provide an event stream (audit log) that records fallback events and estimated quality delta so CS can proactively reach out.

Sample runbook fragment (for oncall)
- Symptom: sudden spike of slim-local decisions for multiple routes in region-us-west-2.
  1) Check pool utilization dashboard for data-plane GPUs.
  2) If utilization > 85% and queue > 200, escalate to infra to scale dedicated capacity.
  3) If peer regions are healthy, confirm spill-routing not blocked by CA policies.
  4) If slim-mode usage rising for paid customers, notify Product Ops and enable auto-rollforward to temporary burst nodes if budget allows.

Open questions and follow-ups (short list):
- How to compute a stable "quality delta" metric that is comparable across model families? (n-gram overlap is insufficient; need human-calibrated eval sets per-route) -> Action: product-research to propose metric by EOD 2024-10-15.
- What's the right default warm-standby sizing? Need simulation based on real QPS traces. -> Action: SRE to run a week-long sim job.
- Billing implications: how do we surface slim-variant cost savings vs customer invoices? -> Action: billing to propose invoice line-item taxonomy.
- Can we make KV-cache keys compatible across slim variants to reduce warmup? That implies serialization compatibility tradeoffs. -> Engineering spike.

Immediate next steps (this doc owner):
- Formalize the contingency matrix template and commit to config proto for control-plane ingestion (INF-2243).
- Start per-model-family slim variant benchmark suite (perf + small eval).
- Add decision-metrics fields to routing-proto PR #87.

Notes to self / improv style comments:
- Keep fallback decisions deterministic and auditable. Avoid ML-driven routing for now; rule-based + score heuristics is easier to reason about.
- We must preserve privacy/data residency constraints as top priority — any cross-border spillover must be opt-in per-account.

References and analogs:
- Past experiments: latency-aware prefilling (internal doc id: perf/warmup-experiments-2023) showed 40% reduction in p95 when slim pool had warm KV for top 10 routes.
- External: some web-cdn vendor whitepapers on tiered cache warmups have good heuristics for prefetch windows.

End of note. This is a draft — comments welcome.
